There Is, There Are in All Forms
Use there is and there are to talk about the things that you can see and the things you know that exist.

You use there is to talk about singular or uncountable nouns that you can see or touch. You use there are for plural countable nouns when you want to refer to its existences or presence.

Affirmative statements 

There is some vital information on that flash drive. (uncountable noun)

There is a model we can use on diverse platforms. (singular noun) 

There are many models we can use when programming. (plural noun)

Negative statements

There isn’t or there is no vital information on that flash drive. (uncountable noun)

There isn’t or there is no a model we can use on diverse platforms. (singular noun)

There aren’t or there are no many models we can use when programming. (plural noun)

Zero Conditional Review
Use the Zero conditional to talk about cause and consequence.

You use the zero conditional to show the result of a possible action, this result always happens if you perform the action you just mentioned.

To form affirmative sentences with the zero conditional use an “if clause” and a “result clause” with two present simple verbs. Follow this structure:

If + subject + present simple, subject + present simple + complement


For example:
If you use OOP, the programming model centers in the objects and not the mathematical logic.

For negative statements there can be a negative result or a negative situation, so you can form it with two different possibilities:

The “if clause” in negative

For example:
If we don't know many programming languages, we use the ones we know to program.

The “result clause” in negative

What is an acronym?
An acronym is a name or a word that you form by putting together the initials of a phrase or words.

You use acronyms as a way to abbreviate and standardize names, some acronyms are used to make it easier to talk about governmental entities or international organizations. Also, you can find some examples of acronyms in software programming,:

OMG: Object Management Group
ORB: Object Request Broker
TPC: Transmission Control Protocol
DCOM: Distributed Component Object Model
CORBA is an acronym that stands for Common Object Request Broker Architecture, this is a standard used for creating and managing distributed program objects in a network.

images.text:
Professor: Today, we're going to talk about CORBA. If you know what CORBA is, raise your hand. Oh, ok. So, I'll explain from the beginning then.
CORBA is an acronym that stands for Common Object Request Broker Architecture, this is a standard used for creating and managing distributed program objects in a network. In other words, it allows programs to develop with different operating systems and with different locations to communicate through an “interface broker”.
Student: Is that the main reason why it is so important?

Professor: Yes. There are many reasons, but the most important one is that CORBA improves the flexibility and portability of the applications. CORBA allows the programmer to work easily without having to go through difficult tasks caused by the heterogeneous computing environment. That's why there aren't many complaints about CORBA. If you use CORBA, you can work with different operating systems, programming languages, and computing hardware.
Student: And, how does CORBA work?

Professor: There is a process where the client program requests services from a server program or object, so the client doesn't need to understand where the server is or what the interface to the server program's looks like. When there are requests or the need to return a reply, programs use the General INTER-ORB protocol. Are there any questions?

Well, there isn't much time left. Tomorrow we will keep explaining everything you need to know about CORBA. If you don't understand something, bring your questions tomorrow so you can pass the test with flying colors.
